title: Telescopes: Optics, Magnification and Resolution
description: Refractor and reflector designs, light grasp, resolution and the magnification formula.
content_html:
Why We Need Telescopes

The human eye has two fundamental limitations as an astronomical instrument: its pupil diameter is only about 7 mm at maximum dilation, restricting the amount of light collected, and it cannot accumulate light over time — it samples the scene afresh every fraction of a second. Telescopes overcome both limitations. A larger aperture collects more light, revealing fainter objects. A camera or CCD sensor attached to a telescope can expose for minutes or hours, allowing very faint detail to build up. Telescopes also magnify, enabling small angular separations on the sky to be resolved.

Refracting and Reflecting Telescopes

There are two fundamental designs based on how they gather and focus light. A refracting telescope (refractor) uses a large convex objective lens to converge parallel rays from a distant object to a focus. The original Galilean telescope (1609) was a refractor. The eyepiece then magnifies the image formed at the focal point. Refractors produce sharp, high-contrast images for planets and the Moon, but suffer from several practical limitations at larger apertures.

A reflecting telescope (reflector) uses a large concave mirror to focus incoming light. The most common design for amateur astronomers is the Newtonian reflector, in which a small flat secondary mirror redirects the focused beam to an eyepiece at the side of the tube. The Cassegrain reflector uses a convex secondary mirror to send the beam back through a hole in the primary mirror to an eyepiece at the rear. Virtually all large professional observatories use reflecting designs, as mirrors can be made much larger than lenses and support from behind, eliminating sag.

Key Fact

Refractors use a convex objective lens; reflectors use a concave mirror. Both focus incoming parallel light rays to a point, after which the eyepiece magnifies the image. Reflectors are preferred for large apertures because mirrors are cheaper, easier to manufacture to high precision, and free from chromatic aberration.

Magnification

The magnification of a telescope is defined as the ratio of the focal length of the objective to the focal length of the eyepiece:

$$M = \frac{f_o}{f_e}$$

where \(M\) is the magnification, \(f_o\) is the focal length of the objective (lens or mirror) and \(f_e\) is the focal length of the eyepiece. A longer objective focal length or shorter eyepiece focal length increases magnification. For example, a telescope with a 1,200 mm objective focal length used with a 6 mm eyepiece produces a magnification of \(M = 1200 / 6 = 200\times\). Swapping to a 20 mm eyepiece reduces magnification to \(M = 1200 / 20 = 60\times\) but gives a wider, brighter field of view.

There is a practical maximum useful magnification for any telescope, roughly 50 times the aperture in inches or 2 times the aperture in millimetres. Beyond this limit, the image becomes too dim and blurred by atmospheric turbulence (seeing) to show extra detail. Higher magnification always means a dimmer image (the same light is spread over a larger area) and a narrower field of view.

Light Grasp and Aperture

The amount of light a telescope collects depends on the area of its objective. Since area scales with the square of diameter:

$$A = \pi \left(\frac{D}{2}\right)^2$$

where \(D\) is the aperture diameter. A telescope with an aperture of 200 mm collects \((200/7)^2 \approx 816\) times more light than the human eye (aperture ~7 mm). Doubling the aperture quadruples the light-gathering area, allowing stars roughly 1.5 magnitudes fainter to be detected. This is why astronomers relentlessly pursue larger apertures: the Extremely Large Telescope (ELT) under construction in Chile will have a 39-metre primary mirror, collecting around 200,000 times more light than the human eye.

Resolution

Resolution is a measure of the finest detail a telescope can distinguish. The minimum angular separation between two objects that can just be resolved depends on the wavelength of light \(\lambda\) and the aperture \(D\):

$$\theta \approx \frac{\lambda}{D}$$

(where \(\theta\) is in radians). A larger aperture resolves finer detail. Longer wavelengths (e.g. radio waves) are harder to resolve than shorter wavelengths (visible light), which is why radio telescopes must be enormously large — or linked into arrays — to match the resolution of an optical telescope of modest size. In practice, Earth's atmosphere limits the resolution of ground-based telescopes to about 1 arcsecond (due to atmospheric turbulence), regardless of aperture size — this is the “seeing” limit.

Chromatic aberration is a defect of lenses only. Glass refracts different wavelengths of light by different amounts — the refractive index varies with wavelength (dispersion). This means different colours in starlight are brought to focus at slightly different points along the optical axis, producing coloured fringes around bright stars and planets. The defect is fundamental to refraction and cannot be eliminated, only reduced using achromatic doublet lenses (two lenses of different glass cemented together). Crucially, mirrors reflect all wavelengths equally — so reflecting telescopes are completely free of chromatic aberration. This is one of the principal reasons professional observatories use reflectors.

Spherical aberration affects mirrors (and lenses). A spherical mirror does not bring all incoming parallel rays to the same focal point — rays near the mirror's edge are focused slightly differently from rays near the centre. The result is a blurred image even in monochromatic light. The Hubble Space Telescope suffered severe spherical aberration when launched in 1990 because its primary mirror was ground to the wrong shape; it was corrected by installing the COSTAR corrective optics in 1993. Spherical aberration is solved by making mirrors parabolic in shape rather than spherical. To summarise the critical distinction: chromatic aberration = lenses, wavelength-dependent refraction; spherical aberration = mirrors or lenses, incorrect shape of the optical surface.

Galileo's Discoveries

Galileo Galilei began systematic telescopic astronomy from 1609 using a Galilean refractor of modest aperture. His discoveries fundamentally changed the understanding of the Solar System: he observed the phases of Venus (proving Venus orbited the Sun inside Earth's orbit), four moons of Jupiter (Io, Europa, Ganymede and Callisto — now called the Galilean moons), mountains and craters on the Moon (showing it was not a perfect sphere), and sunspots (showing the Sun was not perfect and unchanging). These observations provided powerful evidence against the Earth-centred model of the Universe.

Refractors: advantages include a sealed tube (less dust and air turbulence inside), no secondary mirror obstruction reducing light, and high contrast for planetary observing. Disadvantages: chromatic aberration, expensive to manufacture large lenses, glass sags under its own weight for large apertures, and very long tubes are physically impractical above about 100–150 mm aperture.

Reflectors: advantages include no chromatic aberration, mirrors can be made much larger (ground and polished from the rear, supported across their full back surface), shorter tube lengths (mirrors fold the optical path), and lower cost per unit aperture. Disadvantages: mirrors must be periodically re-coated with fresh aluminium, secondary mirrors block some incoming light, and open tubes allow air currents that degrade images (thermal equilibration time).

Key Fact

A telescope’s ability to resolve close-together objects is set by aperture diameter (the diffraction limit θ ≈ λ/D), not by magnification. Two stars 1 arcsecond apart can never be split by a 50mm scope no matter how high the eyepiece magnification — only a bigger aperture fixes it.
exam_tip_html: The magnification formula \(M = f_o / f_e\) appears directly on the formula sheet — always state it before substituting. Show all working: state the formula, substitute values with units, calculate. For light-gathering area questions, use \(A = \pi (D/2)^2\) and compare ratios by squaring diameter ratios. The most common error in aberration questions is claiming chromatic aberration affects reflectors — it does not, because mirrors reflect all wavelengths equally. Chromatic aberration is a lens-only defect. Spherical aberration is a shape defect that can affect both mirrors and lenses.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Refractors use a convex objective lens; Newtonian and Cassegrain reflectors use a concave primary mirror. Both focus parallel rays to a point where the eyepiece magnifies the image.
  • Magnification: \(M = f_o / f_e\). Light-gathering area: \(A = \pi (D/2)^2\) — doubling aperture quadruples light grasp. Resolution improves with larger aperture and shorter wavelength.
  • Chromatic aberration (coloured fringes) is a lens-only defect caused by wavelength-dependent refraction. Reflectors are free of it. Spherical aberration (blurred focus) is a shape defect affecting mirrors and lenses; solved by using parabolic mirrors.
  • Galileo's telescopic observations (phases of Venus, Jovian moons, lunar mountains, sunspots) provided key evidence against the geocentric model of the Solar System.

practice_questions.text:
A telescope has an objective focal length of 900 mm. An eyepiece with a focal length of 25 mm is used.

Calculate the magnification.
practice_questions.marks:
M = f_o / f_e [1 mark]
M = 900 / 25 = 36× [1 mark]
[2 marks]

practice_questions.text: State what type of primary optical element is used in a Newtonian reflecting telescope.

Telescope A has an objective diameter of 60 mm. Telescope B has an objective diameter of 120 mm.

Calculate how many times more light Telescope B collects compared to Telescope A.
practice_questions.marks:
Area A = π × (60/2)² = π × 900 = 2827 mm² [1 mark]
Area B = π × (120/2)² = π × 3600 = 11,310 mm² [1 mark]
Ratio = 11,310 / 2827 = 4 [1 mark]
Conclusion: Telescope B collects 4 times more light. [1 mark]
Alternative method: ratio of areas = (D_B / D_A)² = (120/60)² = 2² = 4. [All 4 marks for correct ratio with clear working]
[4 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain the difference between chromatic aberration and spherical aberration, stating which type of telescope is affected by each.
practice_questions.marks:
Chromatic aberration: caused by wavelength-dependent refraction in lenses — different colours are focused at slightly different distances, producing coloured fringes. [1 mark]
Affects refractors (lenses) only; reflectors (mirrors) are free from it because mirrors reflect all wavelengths equally. [1 mark]
Spherical aberration: caused by an incorrectly shaped optical surface (spherical rather than parabolic) — rays at the mirror or lens edge focus at a slightly different point from central rays, producing a blurred image. [1 mark]
Can affect both refractors and reflectors; corrected by using parabolic mirrors or achromatic lens designs. [1 mark]
[4 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Dr Fiona Ashworth is the director of the Calder Valley Astronomical Society. She is advising a local school on purchasing a first telescope for public observation events. She wants the telescope to show the planets clearly, suffer minimal aberration, and be practical for a school with a limited budget.

Recommend, with justification, a suitable type of telescope. In your answer refer to the advantages of your choice for the specific purposes described.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Clear recommendation with type named; at least three distinct justified points; awareness of limitations addressed; magnification and light grasp principles applied; written fluently. (6 marks)
Secure: Type named and recommended; two or three relevant justifications; some awareness of trade-offs. (4–5 marks)
Developing: Type named; one or two reasons; limited justification. (2–3 marks)
Emerging: Telescope type mentioned but no meaningful justification. (0–1 marks)

Credit points for a Newtonian reflector recommendation:
• No chromatic aberration (mirrors reflect all wavelengths equally) — important for sharp planetary images.
• Larger aperture achievable for a given budget compared to refractors of the same aperture.
• Light-gathering area proportional to aperture squared — more aperture means brighter, more detailed images.
• Secondary mirror obstruction is a minor drawback — affects contrast slightly.
• Open tube requires settling time in cold air before use.
• Mirrors need periodic re-aligning (collimation) and re-coating — requires some maintenance.

Credit for refractor recommendation if well-justified:
• Sealed tube reduces internal air currents, giving steadier images.
• No secondary mirror obstruction — high contrast for Moon and bright planets.
• Low maintenance. Chromatic aberration manageable with achromatic doublet lenses at modest aperture.
• Limited to smaller apertures on a school budget.

practice_questions.text: Explain two telescopic discoveries made by Galileo Galilei and explain how each one challenged the Earth-centred model of the Universe.
practice_questions.marks:
Two credit points, each worth up to 1.5 marks (round to nearest mark):
• Phases of Venus: Galileo observed that Venus showed a full cycle of phases (like the Moon), including a full phase. This is only possible if Venus orbits the Sun inside Earth's orbit. In the Earth-centred model, Venus could not show a full phase, so this directly contradicted the geocentric view. [1–2 marks depending on depth]
• Four moons of Jupiter (Galilean moons — Io, Europa, Ganymede, Callisto): Galileo observed four points of light orbiting Jupiter, not Earth. This proved not all bodies in the Universe revolved around Earth, contradicting a key assumption of the geocentric model. [1–2 marks depending on depth]
[3 marks total, split across both discoveries]

knowledge_checks.q: A telescope has an objective focal length of 600 mm and an eyepiece focal length of 10 mm. What is the magnification?
Chromatic aberration only affects _____ telescopes because lenses refract different wavelengths by different amounts.
Which formula correctly gives the magnification of a telescope?
options: M = focal length of objective ÷ focal length of eyepiece
M = focal length of eyepiece ÷ focal length of objective
M = aperture diameter ÷ focal length of eyepiece
M = focal length of objective × focal length of eyepiece

knowledge_checks.q: The light-gathering area of a telescope is proportional to the _____ of the aperture diameter.
Match each optical defect to its cause.
right: Wavelength-dependent refraction in a lens — fixed with achromatic or reflector designs
Spherical mirror shape — fixed by using a parabolic mirror
Wave nature of light — set by aperture size, no full fix

flashcard_questions.q: What is the magnification formula for a telescope?
flashcard_questions.a: M = focal length of objective ÷ focal length of eyepiece (M = f_o / f_e).

flashcard_questions.q: What optical element does a refractor use as its objective?
What optical element does a reflector use as its objective?

flashcard_questions.a: Glass refracts different wavelengths by different amounts, focusing colours at different points.

flashcard_questions.q: Which telescope type is free of chromatic aberration and why?
flashcard_questions.a: Reflectors — mirrors reflect all wavelengths equally, so no wavelength-dependent focusing error occurs.
A defect caused by an incorrectly shaped optical surface where edge rays focus differently from central rays.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the formula for the light-gathering area of a telescope objective?
flashcard_questions.a: A = π(D/2)²  where D is aperture diameter.

flashcard_questions.q: How does doubling aperture affect light grasp?
flashcard_questions.a: It quadruples the light-gathering area (area scales with diameter squared).

flashcard_questions.q: What limits resolution in practice for ground-based telescopes?
flashcard_questions.a: Atmospheric turbulence (seeing), limiting resolution to about 1 arcsecond regardless of aperture.

flashcard_questions.q: Name two of Galileo's telescopic discoveries.
flashcard_questions.a: Any two of: phases of Venus, four moons of Jupiter, lunar mountains and craters, sunspots.

flashcard_questions.q: What design is the Newtonian reflector?
flashcard_questions.a: A concave primary mirror + flat secondary mirror that redirects light to an eyepiece at the side of the tube.

flashcard_questions.q: Why are large refracting telescopes impractical?
flashcard_questions.a: Large lenses are expensive to make, sag under their own weight, and produce chromatic aberration.

glossary_terms.definition: A telescope that uses a large convex objective lens to focus incoming light.
A telescope that uses a large concave mirror to focus incoming light.
The distance from the centre of a lens or mirror to the point where parallel rays are brought to focus.
The ratio of the objective focal length to the eyepiece focal length: M = f_o / f_e.
The amount of light a telescope collects, proportional to the area of its objective (A = π(D/2)²).
The ability of a telescope to distinguish fine angular detail; improves with larger aperture and shorter wavelength.
A lens defect in which different wavelengths of light are focused at different points, producing coloured fringes. Reflectors are free of this defect.
An optical defect where rays from the edge of a spherical mirror or lens are focused at a different point from central rays; corrected by using a parabolic surface.

items.description: Christopher Nolan's film used real astrophysics to render the black hole Gargantua — a superb example of how telescope data and computer modelling combine.
